**Monday, February 29, 1960**

You arrived on one of the rarest dates on the calendar — a day that exists only once every four years, inserted into February by the slow accounting of our planet's orbit. In 66 years of life, you have had sixteen true birthdays. Most people your age have had 66. The date itself is a small wonder. And the world outside was not quiet when you arrived.

---

**The Agadir earthquake — exact date**

On the night of February 29, 1960, the ground beneath Agadir, Morocco convulsed. The earthquake struck around 11:40 PM local time — late enough that most of the city's population was asleep when buildings collapsed around them. In less than fifteen seconds, roughly a third of Agadir's residents were dead: somewhere between 12,000 and 15,000 people, in a city of 35,000. The earthquake was not exceptionally powerful by seismic standards, but it was shallow, and the city was not built to survive it. Agadir had to be rebuilt entirely from scratch, on a new plan, in a new location. Across the world, the day that became your birthday was, for an entire city, a day of catastrophe.

---

**The day after Squaw Valley — exact-date timing**

The day before you were born, the 1960 Winter Olympics closed at Squaw Valley, California — the first Winter Games hosted in the American West, and the first to be televised in the United States. CBS broadcast the events into living rooms across the country. The American ice hockey team — college-age players given no chance — won gold, a performance that prefigured the Miracle on Ice twenty years later. You were born the day after the closing ceremony, into a country still buzzing with something that had just ended.

---

**The Year of Africa — the world remaking its map**

Nineteen sixty was the Year of Africa. Seventeen nations gained independence that calendar year — a wave of decolonization that reshaped the world map more dramatically in a single year than almost any other event of the twentieth century. Congo, Nigeria, Senegal, Mali, Ivory Coast, and more: countries that had existed as European possessions for generations were becoming sovereign states. The process was often chaotic — Congo erupted into crisis within weeks of independence — but it was irreversible. The world you entered was shedding the last formal architecture of empire.

---

**Kennedy's year — the American political moment**

John F. Kennedy had announced his presidential candidacy just eight weeks before you were born. He was 42, Catholic, a senator — and running against the assumption that someone like him could not be president. By November he had won, defeating Nixon in one of the closest elections in American history. Kennedy's election announced something: the postwar generation was taking the controls, television had arrived in politics, and a particular American confidence — young, forward-leaning, shaped by the space race — was about to set the national tone for a decade. You were born in the last weeks of Eisenhower's America. You grew up in what followed.

---

**±30-day worldwide event: France's first nuclear test — February 13, 1960, sixteen days before your birth**

Sixteen days before you were born, France detonated its first atomic bomb in the Sahara Desert — code-named *Gerboise Bleue* — joining the United States, the Soviet Union, and Britain as the world's fourth nuclear power. The test was an act of deliberate assertion by Charles de Gaulle: France would not depend on American nuclear protection; France would have its own deterrent; France would answer to no one. The explosion intensified pressure on non-nuclear nations, accelerated calls for a test-ban treaty, and planted the seed of what would eventually become the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The world you were born into was one in which the club of nations capable of ending civilization was still growing.

---

**The lifetime that followed**

You have had sixteen birthdays. In those sixteen, and the 66 years they span: you were nine when Armstrong walked on the Moon. Twenty-three when HIV/AIDS was named and no one yet knew what it was or where it came from. Twenty-nine when the Berlin Wall fell on live television — the same medium that had broadcast the Squaw Valley Olympics the day before you were born. Forty-one on September 11, 2001. Sixty when the pandemic began.

In 66 years: the contraceptive pill, satellite communication, the personal computer, the internet, the human genome sequenced, gene editing, the smartphone, and now artificial intelligence capable of conversation. The world of February 1960 — its Cold War conducted between two superpowers building ever-larger arsenals, its Africa just emerging from colonial rule, its computers reserved for governments and universities — is another world entirely.

---

**What kind of world did you enter?**

You were born on a day that barely exists, in a year that was remaking the globe. The world of February 29, 1960 was one of enormous, simultaneous motion: empires dissolving, a new American presidency forming, the nuclear club expanding, television becoming the medium through which humanity would come to experience itself. The Agadir earthquake, the Squaw Valley closing ceremony, the French bomb in the Sahara sixteen days prior — none of these knew about each other, and none of them knew about you.

Sixty-six years and sixteen birthdays later, you are the only one still keeping track.
